lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: This one. See the leaves? Three points, serrated edge, alternating on the stem.

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.text: Trifoliate arrangement. That's consistent with the Apiaceae family — possibly a wild chervil variant.

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: It's food. You can eat the leaves raw or boil the root. Tastes like parsley if parsley were apologetic about existing.

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.monologue: She describes flavor profiles the way I describe historical periods. With specificity and without mercy.

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: And this one. Don't touch this one.

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: Same family, different manners. This one will make you sick for three days. See how the stem is purple at the base? That's how you know.

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.text: So the distinguishing feature between the edible and the toxic variety is stem coloration? That seems like it should be documented more precisely. If I could take a sample back to the archive—

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: It is documented. I just documented it. I said 'purple stem means bad.' That's the document.

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.text: But without a formal classification system, how does the knowledge transfer? What if something happens to you?

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: Then someone else who grew up in a forest will look at the purple stem and not eat it. Because they'll be the kind of person who knows that things with purple stems in this region are usually the kind of thing you don't put in your mouth.
lines.monologue: He's writing in his notebook. Of course he is. He probably has a section labeled 'Field Botany — Informal Classification Systems.'

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.text: I'm not saying your system is wrong.

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.text: I'm saying it could be more complete.

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: And I'm saying it doesn't matter what family the plant is in. It matters if it'll make you sick.
lines.monologue: He pauses. His pen stops. That's how I know I've gotten through — when the pen stops.

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.monologue: She's right. And I'm right. The knowledge that keeps you alive in the field is not the same as the knowledge that keeps a civilization from forgetting what it knew. Both kinds matter. I'm just better at one of them.

lines.speaker: Lex
lines.text: Teach me the purple stem rule. I'll write it down your way and my way. Both versions.

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.monologue: That's — actually reasonable. I didn't expect reasonable. I expected another ten minutes of him trying to Latinize the word 'root.'

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.text: Fine. Next one. See the berries on this shrub?

lines.speaker: Rynn
lines.monologue: I eat three. I hand him three. He eats them with the expression of a man who is fighting very hard not to say 'antioxidant properties.' I appreciate the effort.
